summary: An experimental document that defines a standard format for representing detached DNS information, intended for storing information retrieved from the DNS, including security information, in archives or contexts not connected to the Internet.

eli5.summary: This is a way to save a copy of phone-book answers in a file, so they can be checked or used later even without internet.

questions: how to store dns answers offline
subtitle: A format for storing DNS answers offline with timestamps.

tldr.problem: DNS information is normally looked up live from the internet, but sometimes you need to preserve and verify DNS answers after the fact, such as for archival or security purposes.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a standard format for recording DNS resource records with timestamps, in both binary and text forms, so they can be stored offline and checked for authenticity later.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can maintain signed archives of DNS data and use them to verify historical records or check information when the network is unavailable.

today: RFC 2540 remains Experimental. Modern DNSSEC implementations use different mechanisms for storing and verifying signed DNS data. However, the format is still useful for archival purposes and for preserving historical DNS records.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the distributed database that translates internet hostnames to IP addresses. Normally, you look up a name every time you need it, and the answer might be different each time (the record might change, or you might get a different server). However, sometimes you need to keep a copy of a DNS answer permanently—for example, to prove that a website existed at a particular time, or to verify the authenticity of a record after the fact.

This RFC defines how to save DNS answers in a standard format, along with the time they were retrieved. The format includes both a binary (machine-readable) version and a text (human-readable) version.
sections.eli5: This is a way to save what the DNS server said, and when it said it. You can keep these copies and check them later.

sections.title: Binary and Text Formats
sections.content:
The binary format stores detached DNS information as a sequence of blocks, each containing a retrieval time and zero or more DNS resource records (RRs) that were fetched at that time. Each block begins with a 32-bit retrieval time (seconds since 1 January 1970 GMT), followed by a 16-bit count of RRs, then the RRs themselves in the same binary format used by DNS messages. Multiple blocks can follow, each with its own timestamp and set of RRs. The end of the data is marked by a retrieval time field starting with the byte 0x20 (32 decimal).

The text format uses the standard DNS zone file format (as defined in RFC 1035) with one addition: a new $DATE entry that specifies the retrieval time in the form YYYYMMDDHHMMSS. A $DATE must appear before the first resource record and at each change of retrieval time.
sections.eli5: The binary version is a compact record: the time, a count of answers, then the answers. The text version is a readable file that looks like a DNS zone file but has date stamps.

sections.title: Freshness and Validity
sections.content:
Unlike live DNS, where a server forgets old records when their Time To Live (TTL) expires, detached DNS information is stored offline and the TTL is not counted down. Instead, the validity of a record is determined by comparing the current time to the retrieval time plus the original TTL. If current_time - retrieval_time > TTL, the record is considered stale according to normal DNS rules.

Additionally, if a resource record is a digital signature (a SIG RR in DNSSEC), the signature has its own expiration time. Even if the TTL has not expired, the signature cannot be trusted after its signature expiration time.

This approach allows detached DNS information to be used for historical verification: you can see what the DNS said on a particular date, and verify whether that information was supposed to be authoritative at that time.
sections.eli5: A saved DNS answer gets stale just like the live one would, but you record when you saved it so you can calculate when it went stale.

sections.title: Use Cases and Security
sections.content:
One common use case is building an authenticated chain for DNSSEC verification. If you retrieve a key record and the signature on that key from the DNS, you can save both. Later, to prove that a document was signed with a particular key at a particular time, you present the archived DNS records along with the signature. The verifier can check that the key was legitimate at that time by verifying the signature with that key, and confirming that the key was not expired.

The detached format itself does not provide security; it is just a container. Security comes from the digital signatures inside the DNS records (SIG RRs) or from wrapping the entire detached information block with another signature.

An important limitation: the detached format does not prevent an attacker from replacing the entire file with a different one. It only allows verification of records that include their own digital signatures. Therefore, it is recommended that the detached information be further signed or protected when it is used for important purposes.
sections.eli5: You can use saved DNS answers to prove something was true on a certain date. You can also wrap them in a signature to prevent someone from tampering with the saved file.

sections.title: Reserved and Future Extensions
sections.content:
The binary format reserves retrieval time values with an initial byte between 0x01 and 0x1F for future use. The initial byte 0x20 marks the end of the data. All other initial bytes (0x21 and higher) represent normal 32-bit retrieval times, which covers all timestamps from March 1985 onward.

When timestamps exceed the 32-bit limit (sometime in the year 2106), a 64-bit format will be needed: an initial byte of 0x00, followed by 8 zero bits and a 56-bit timestamp, allowing dates far into the future.

Assignment of meanings to the reserved range (0x01 to 0x1F) requires IETF consensus.
sections.eli5: The format saves room for future improvements. If computers need to handle dates after 2106, a longer timestamp format is available.
